“An ordinary residential building was destroyed in Kharkiv; the rescue operation continued virtually all night as first responders searched for people under the rubble. Four people were killed in this strike on the building in Kharkiv. My condolences to all their families and loved ones. In Kharkiv alone, 41 people were injured in just one evening.

US ‌president Donald Trump had said on Monday that he was considering firing Guilfoyle, telling reporters: “We’re not happy.“

Well: the White House has just confirmed she has been asked to resign from the post.
“We have ‌asked Ambassador ‌Guilfoyle to resign,” said White House new press secretary ‌ Katie Zacharia . “She has been a wonderful asset ⁠to the ​team, and ​we ​wish her ​well.“
The news immediately made the splash on various Greek news websites, including Kathimerini.

Photograph: John Leicester/AP “Young people are not being included in the conversation,” Thunberg, 23, who became famous as a teenager through school strikes demanding action on the climate crisis, told reporters outside the Lycée Paul Éluard in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis.
As lawyers in their robes formed a human chain to protect pupils after multiple accusations of police brutality , she added: “ Our future is being stolen from us and, as we have seen here, schools are not getting the investment they need.”
Students march to protest against under-resourced schools in Rennes, France. Photograph: Jeremías González/AP Now in their third week, the protests – backed by unionists, some teachers and radical leftwing opposition politicians – have shaken a government caught between calls for urgent public investment and pressure to reduce France’s ballooning deficit and debt.

Finnish prime minister Petteri Orpo attends a meeting in Rovaniemi, Finland. He added that such a deal “funds Putin’s war” against Ukraine.
The Finnish prime minister urged Europe and Ukraine’s supporters to “say this forcefully to Trump”.
“Continuing support for Ukraine is now more essential than ever,” he added.
The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, called for tougher measures to curb illegal migration in a letter sent to the 27 leaders of the EU member countries ahead of a discussion on the topic scheduled for Friday.
She said this summer’s huge border crossing of migrants from Morocco into Ceuta – in which about 140 people are estimated to have died – showed just how quickly “sudden massive arrivals can put pressure on the EU’s external borders”.
Her proposals include broadening the powers of the EU’s border agency, Frontex, including a new “Quick Reaction Force for crisis deployment”, and increasing the bloc’s return rate.
The European Parliament in June approved an overhaul of migration policy aimed at speeding up deportations and allowing ​member states to establish centres abroad, in what critics warned could weaken safeguards for asylum seekers.
As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta at the end of July and the start of August. As regards specifically this question on Russian diesel exports, if we look at the volumes, they are not of any macroeconomic significance, and frankly, there are strong doubts whether Russia is even able to supply those volumes , and according also to US quality standards, those are big question marks.

Saudi Arabia Plans Massive Expansion of Oil Pipeline to Bypass Hormuz
Saudi Arabia plans to raise the capacity of its East-West onshore oil pipeline that helps it bypass the Strait of Hormuz to 10 million barrels per day (bpd) within two to three years, Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said at the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh.
The pipeline, which returned to service after a two-week suspension following drone attacks in September, currently carries about 5.8 million bpd, the minister said last week.
The 740-mile-long pipeline, also known as Petroline, has a maximum capacity of 7 million bpd at present.
Despite the ongoing conflict and disruptions, Saudi Arabia plans to add 3 million bpd to the East-West pipeline, which became a lifeline for Saudi oil exports after the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
Thanks to the pipeline, Saudi Arabia managed to divert most of its crude oil exports away from the choked Strait of Hormuz and ships increasingly larger volumes via the Yanbu port on the Red Sea.
The route to bypass Hormuz is not without risks, either. The Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen vowed in July to halt Saudi shipments through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which is the shortest route for Saudi oil supply from Yanbu to reach Asian markets.
Still, Prince Abdulaziz on Monday touted the energy resilience of the Kingdom, telling the WPC Energy Congress that energy resilience "must also be measured by the ability to maintain, repair, reroute, substitute and recover. Above all, it must be measured by the ability to continue delivering under pressure."
Saudi Aramco's chief executive officer, Amin Nasser, said at the same event that "In alignment with the Ministry of Energy, we are studying additional crude export routes, and working on expanding overseas storage."
Aramco's top executive added that the company is "also focused on mitigating risks and limiting damage, using frontier technologies to inspect facilities and accelerate restoration."

Allies did not warn Kyiv of Russian ballistic missile strikes, says Zelenskyy
Ukrainian president’s comments on ‘particularly vile’ strikes come after US threatened to halt intelligence sharing
Ukraine received no early warning from its partners about a Russian ballistic missile strike on Kyiv in which five missiles hit civilian infrastructure, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday.
The Ukrainian president described the attack on Monday as “particularly vile”. He emphasised that receiving intelligence from Ukraine’s western allies “helps saves lives, and this is one of the most critical issues”.
“This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed – when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles,” he wrote on social media . He did not apportion blame for the lack of warning, calling it unfortunate.
US officials made explicit threats over the weekend to their Ukrainian counterparts that the Trump administration was on the brink of halting intelligence sharing with Kyiv. However, speaking in Warsaw, Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, indicated that cooperation was continuing and said the lack of warning over the Kyiv attack was due to a “special type” of Russian weaponry.
Donald Trump has demanded that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil refineries and has blamed Zelenskyy for the rise in fuel prices in the US. On Friday the US president announced a deal with Vladimir Putin to import diesel from Russia, dropping previous US sanctions.
He also claimed Moscow and Kyiv had agreed an “energy ceasefire”, something Zelenskyy described as “news to me” . On Tuesday Ukraine’s leader said his military had not struck Russian oil refineries or energy facilities in the two days following Trump’s Sunday announcement.
The Kremlin, however, had ignored the “ceasefire” and continued to bomb Ukraine’s energy infrastructure as before, with multiple attacks, he said. “Russia did not heed the president … The Russians sent absolutely clear signals that they have no intention of refraining from strikes,” he noted.
Ukrainian commanders say American intelligence is not needed to identify targets for deep strikes on Russia , with oil refineries marked on Google Maps. But they say it plays a crucial role in warning of Russian ballistic missile launches, and the takeoff of long-range bomber aircraft.
In recent months Russia has dramatically stepped up its bombardment of Ukrainian towns and cities. Ukraine has struggled to shoot down incoming missiles and jet-powered drones and has appealed to partners to boost its dwindling supplies of US-made Patriot missiles.
According to the Financial Times , the Trump administration has also threatened to suspend the procurement scheme under which Ukraine’s European allies buy advanced US systems, which are then sent to Kyiv, including badly needed Patriots.
The Kremlin’s systematic campaign against Ukraine’s power grid has led to widespread blackouts in Kyiv and other cities. Putin’s apparent goal is to shut off heating and electricity for millions of civilians this winter, and to trigger a new wave of refugees into neighbouring EU states.
On Monday Russia bombarded the city of Kharkiv, destroying a residential building. Sharing footage from the scene, Zelenskyy said four people had been killed and 41 injured. Rescuers spent the entire night searching for people trapped under the rubble, he added.
The row between Washington and Kyiv is the most serious since last year, when Trump threw Zelenskyy out of the White House. Ukraine’s president has said he is willing to stop hitting Russian oil refineries – but only on a reciprocal basis and with “real guarantees” that Moscow will cease its attacks on Ukraine’s own energy sites.
“Direct or indirect support for Russia, delaying aid to Ukraine, and complicating protection of lives from ballistics – this is what will definitely not work for peace. A strong America, a strong Europe , strong partners are needed,” he said on Tuesday.

Iranian attacks target 6 ships near Strait of Hormuz in 1 day, highest since war with US began
Iranian attacks target 6 ships near Strait of Hormuz in 1 day, highest since war with US began
More than 18 vessels targeted during first 12 days of October, according to UK maritime agency, international security sources
Ahmet Dursun, Mohammad Kara Maryam, and Lina Altawell
ISTANBUL Iranian attacks on vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz have reached their highest pace since the war with the US began on Feb. 28, with six ships targeted in a single day, according to data from the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency (UKMTO) and international maritime security sources.
Data from UKMTO and maritime security sources showed that more than 18 commercial vessels were targeted by Iran during the first 12 days of October, including six on Monday.
Between Oct. 5 and 12 alone, at least 14 attacks, attempted attacks and interceptions involving vessels were recorded in and around the strait, according to the same sources.
UKMTO data and statements by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) indicated a marked rise in attacks on commercial shipping since clashes between Tehran and Washington resumed in July.
At least 12 attacks on oil tankers and cargo ships were recorded in July, while at least 10 vessels were targeted in August, including oil and liquefied natural gas tankers off the UAE port of Fujairah and Oman’s Sohar.
The number rose to 18 vessels in September as the US and Gulf countries increasingly resorted to ship-to-ship transfers, using smaller vessels to transport oil before loading it onto larger tankers in safer areas.
The IRGC claimed that the operations were “illegal oil smuggling and an attempt to break the Hormuz blockade” and expanded its operations to include supply vessels, tugboats and small tankers in the Gulf.
The IRGC also claimed that some targeted vessels were damaged by explosions after striking naval mines while sailing “illegally” through routes it considered “unsafe.”
Tehran says the escalation in its operations against shipping is a response to a “US naval blockade,” while warning vessels against using routes it has not approved or crossing the area after switching off navigation and identification systems.
Since April, Iran has imposed restrictions on maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, including designated transit routes and a requirement for prior coordination with the IRGC Navy.
On May 30, Tehran announced that vessels passing through the strait would be required to obtain prior authorization from the IRGC Navy, warning that transit without permission would constitute a “security threat.”
The developments come amid continued tensions between Iran and the US over navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important strategic routes for energy and commodity supplies and a key issue in negotiations between the two sides.
​​​​​​​The war began with US and Israeli attacks on Iran on Feb. 28, before a ceasefire was reached in April. Clashes between Washington and Tehran later resumed as negotiations stalled despite the two sides signing a memorandum of understanding in June.

items.title: Russia's offensive ability is broken, Kyiv's former top general tells BBC
items.summary: In his first interview since being forced from his post, Gen Syrskyi speaks about Ukraine's future in the war.
items.content:
Image caption, Gen Syrskyi, pictured here in Donetsk region in April 2026, lost his job over the summer after a public disagreement with the defence minister
Ukraine has stabilised the front line and "broken Russia's ability to advance" by killing so many of its men, Ukraine's former commander-in-chief has said in an interview with the BBC.
Gen Oleksandr Syrskyi made the comments in an exclusive interview, his first since he was dramatically forced from his post in the summer.
He addressed his sacking, disagreeing with his critics who declared him too "old school" to command Ukraine's new, technologically advanced forces.
He also pushed back against allegations made by soldiers who previously served under him, who told the BBC they were ordered to remain at their positions even when they were almost surrounded by Russians, leading to high losses.
Syrskyi said that Moscow's overall losses in the war were six times higher than Ukraine's. "If you count only dead, then it's up to 11 times," he added.
Neither Russia nor Ukraine officially release the numbers of their dead. Ukraine's military says it inflicted record losses this year on Russian soldiers in September, although that cannot be verified.
UK intelligence chiefs estimate Russia has lost around half a million men killed in Ukraine since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022. The US-based Center for Strategic and International Studies meanwhile believes , external Ukraine has lost up to 150,000 troops killed by June 2026.
He says this difference in death toll â as well as technological advances, and a strategy of attacking weak points in Russia's lines while containing their advances in other parts â accounts for the current stalemate at the front.
In the first six months of 2026, Russia managed overall to seize 61 sq km, the general said. "It's an indication that the front line has been stabilised."
The Institute for Study of War (ISW) has also confirmed this trend. One of its recent reports , external says that in September 2026, Moscow lost more territory than it took.
Syrskyi was appointed Ukraine's commander-in-chief in 2024. He had previously won praise for defending Kyiv at the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, and for leading the successful counteroffensive east of Kharkiv in the autumn of that year.
But President Volodymyr Zelensky fired Syrskyi this summer, amid a major disagreement with then-defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov.
Fedorov had said that instead of adapting to the realities of the changing war, the army under Syrskyi had blocked his initiatives.
Zelensky initially fired Fedorov, as tensions burst into the open between the two men. But mass street protests then forced the president to also fire Syrskyi, replacing him with Maj Gen Mykhailo Drapatyi, 43.
Syrskyi told the BBC that he had "disagreements" with Fedorov because the latter "didn't take into consideration the interests of the army" when procuring weapons and supplies.
Fedorov had created an "imbalance" in supplies, Syrskyi said. He had prioritised drones while overlooking key front-line kit such as unmanned ground vehicles, pick-up trucks and motorbikes. Even with drones, Syrskyi said, there were shortages as the army got only half of what they needed.
Fedorov was a popular young minister who was known for his digital and technological initiatives. Many contrasted him with Syrskyi, who critics thought was not fit to lead the new technological arms race with Russia.
But Syrskyi disagrees with such criticism. It was during his time the use of drones reached this new, unprecedented level, including deep strikes more than 2,000km (1,200 miles) behind enemy lines, he said. Ukraine was the first country to create the Unmanned Systems Forces as a separate branch of armed forces, under his command: now, he said, drones account for 80% of Russia's losses.
Image caption, Gen Syrskyi was appointed commander-in-chief of the armed forces in 2024
Under his military leadership, however, Ukrainian troops undertook chaotic withdrawals from the eastern cities of Avdiivka and Vuhledar, and from around Pokrovsk.
Soldiers who spoke to the BBC in the past complained that they were ordered to remain at their positions at any costs. By the time they were told to pull back, it was often too late as they were almost surrounded by Russian troops.
Syrskyi does not deny that such situations occur on the front line. But he told the BBC that Ukraine was fighting against a far more powerful army.
In 2025, the ratio of jets and bombs was 18 to one in Moscow's favour, he said. In the same year, Russia had two-and-a-half times more artillery pieces and shells than Ukraine. And with four million militarily trained men who they can mobilise, Russian forces can create chances to push through, he argued.
One of Syrskyi's most famous operations was an incursion into Russia's Kursk region that started in August 2024. It ended with a dramatic retreat the following spring, which some soldiers described as "catastrophic". Syrskyi, however, insisted that the Kursk operation was "a necessity".
"In the summer 2024, Russian forces were pushing along all main directions on the front line with up to six times more troops than we had," he explained.
The Kursk incursion disrupted Russia's offensive and forced Moscow to redirect troops, giving Ukraine a respite and a chance for its stretched brigades in the east and south to recover, Syrskyi said.
He also had strong words for European allies who doubt that Russia may have territorial ambitions beyond Ukraine. He advised European partners to start preparing for the war now and "drop all illusions that [it] will not come".
He also said he believed Ukraine's war was going to become even more technological. There will be more robots, automated systems and artificial intelligence (AI). "Even ordinary weapons now get an AI-based control system to enhance their capabilities," he said.
Such technologies can give a new life to conventional weapons like tanks. Both Russia and Ukraine were now racing to develop "active systems of defence" to protect armoured vehicles, Syrskyi said.
But he insisted that "the human role will remain definitive [on the battlefield] because [people] will need to control those systems".

items.content:
Gold Prices Rise as Oil Retreats Ahead of US Inflation Data and Federal Reserve Decision
Gold bars ©Adobe Stock Images Gold prices moved higher on Tuesday as a decline in crude oil prices provided some support for the precious metal, while investors assessed inflation risks linked to the Middle East conflict and awaited US consumer price data.
At 04:47 ET (08:47 GMT), spot gold (XAU/USD) advanced 0.4% to $4,189.12 an ounce, while gold futures gained 0.5% to $4,213.25 an ounce.
The recovery came as oil prices retreated following indications that Russia could increase diesel exports beyond previously announced volumes under a supply agreement with the United States.
However, crude prices remained elevated amid concerns about disruptions to energy shipments from the Gulf, particularly following attacks attributed to Iran-backed Houthi forces on Saudi Arabia's international airport in Riyadh.
The developments have complicated the outlook for gold, which has traditionally attracted demand during periods of geopolitical uncertainty but can also come under pressure when rising energy costs increase inflation expectations and encourage tighter monetary policy.
Middle East Conflict and Oil Prices Influence Gold Market
The continuing conflict in the Middle East has created competing influences on precious metal prices.
Geopolitical instability can support demand for gold as investors seek assets perceived as relatively defensive during periods of uncertainty.
However, higher oil prices can also contribute to persistent inflation, potentially prompting central banks to maintain elevated interest rates or introduce further increases.
Gold has declined by approximately 20% since the United States and Israel launched a joint military assault on Iran in late February, according to the reported market figures.
The decline has reflected concerns that rising energy prices could prolong inflationary pressures and lead to additional monetary tightening.
Higher interest rates generally increase the opportunity cost of holding gold because the metal does not generate interest income.
As a result, interest-bearing assets such as government bonds can become relatively more attractive when borrowing costs and yields rise.
Tuesday's decline in oil prices offered some relief from these concerns, although uncertainty surrounding Middle Eastern energy supplies continued to influence market sentiment.
The possibility of increased Russian diesel exports could help ease pressure on global fuel markets, but risks to Gulf shipping routes remain an important consideration for traders.
Central Bank Purchases Support Longer-Term Gold Demand
Despite recent price weakness, continued purchases by central banks remain an important source of underlying demand for gold.
Analysts at The Gold Bullion Company highlighted the role of official-sector buying in supporting the precious metal's longer-term outlook.
Central banks have continued adding gold to their reserves as part of efforts to diversify their holdings and reduce exposure to individual reserve assets.
According to the analysts, these purchases allow countries to "diversify their reserves and reduce dependence on any single reserve asset", including the US dollar.
Gold's role as a reserve asset remains relevant for monetary authorities seeking to manage currency exposure and maintain a diversified portfolio of international assets.
Such demand can provide longer-term support for bullion, although short-term price movements remain sensitive to interest rates, currency fluctuations and geopolitical developments.
US Inflation Figures Could Shape Federal Reserve Policy
Investors were preparing for the release of US consumer price inflation data on Wednesday, with the figures expected to provide further insight into the Federal Reserve's monetary policy outlook.
The central bank raised interest rates in September for the first time since 2023, citing the need to contain inflation.
However, expectations have shifted towards the possibility that policymakers will leave borrowing costs unchanged at their October meeting.
Interest-rate swaps indicated an approximately 20% probability of another increase in October, although financial markets continued to anticipate one additional rate rise before the end of 2026.
The forthcoming inflation report could influence those expectations, particularly if consumer prices show evidence of continued pressure from higher energy costs.
A stronger-than-expected inflation reading could reinforce expectations for restrictive monetary policy, potentially weighing on gold.
Conversely, signs of easing price pressures could reduce expectations for further tightening and improve the outlook for non-yielding assets.
Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Beth Hammack said on Monday that smaller, more frequent monetary policy adjustments could help maintain stable inflation expectations.
However, she did not explicitly support an interest-rate increase at the Fed's October meeting.
Her comments highlighted the importance of incoming economic data as policymakers assess the appropriate pace of any additional adjustments.
Other precious metals also advanced during Tuesday's session.
Spot silver rose 0.3% to $60.4830 an ounce, while spot platinum increased 0.7% to $1,704.03 an ounce.
The broader gains coincided with weakness in the US dollar.
The US Dollar Index, which measures the currency against a basket of major international counterparts, declined 0.3% to 102.33.
A weaker dollar can make gold and other dollar-denominated commodities less expensive for buyers using foreign currencies, potentially supporting international demand.
Currency movements therefore provided an additional favourable influence on precious metal prices during the session.
Gold Outlook Remains Dependent on Inflation and Interest Rates
Gold's modest recovery reflected a combination of lower oil prices, dollar weakness and continued uncertainty surrounding the global economic outlook.
However, the metal remains exposed to competing influences from geopolitical risk and expectations for US monetary policy.
Persistent energy supply disruptions could increase demand for defensive assets, but they could also sustain inflation and raise the likelihood of additional interest-rate increases.
The upcoming US consumer price report will therefore be an important indicator for investors assessing the Federal Reserve's next steps.
Beyond the immediate inflation figures, central bank purchases and reserve diversification are expected to remain important considerations for the longer-term gold market.

Trump’s Russian diesel deal won’t change US oil markets much: Analysis
Russia has claimed it can supply even more diesel to the global market than the quantities agreed with United States President Donald Trump.
“By the end of the year, we could reach supply volumes of 3.5 million tonnes per month to global markets, just as was the case before the crisis,” Alexander Novak, Russian deputy prime minister, told the news programme Vesti on Monday.
list of 4 items list 1 of 4 Ukraine warns Trump-Putin diesel deal will bankroll Russia’s war
list 2 of 4 ‘Energy ceasefire’: What’s behind Trump’s love-hate ties to Russian oil?
list 3 of 4 From a ‘dangerous competitor’ to an unknown: Who could replace Zelenskyy?
list 4 of 4 Trump insists energy ceasefire holds as Ukraine reports new Russian strikes
President Vladimir Putin and Trump spoke on Friday on an agreement expected to bring 300,000 tonnes of diesel to global markets in October, half a million tonnes in November, and a million tonnes in December.
“Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!” Trump posted.
But experts are sceptical, and the move has opened a rift between the US and Europe on the Ukraine war.
Kostis Stambolis, executive director of the Institute of Energy for South-East Europe (IENE), described the US move as “purely political” and designed to put Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in a corner.
Trump wants to signal that the US has “no problem with Russia”, unlike Europe, he said.
“Russia produces 5.8 million tonnes of diesel a month. Two million are likely to be available for export,” he added.
Europe has reacted to the diesel deal by backing Ukraine, whose war funding will be “front and centre” of this week’s European Council summit, European Commission President Ursula Von Der Leyen said on Sunday.
Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen on Monday called on Europeans to ban all tourist visas to Russians.
Stambolis believes Trump was leveraging European weakness to shift its position on Ukraine.
“About 30 European refineries have closed in the past 15 years for environmental reasons, because they have to pay to emit greenhouse gases,” he said, referring to Europe’s Emissions Trading Scheme, “so now Europe is not self-sufficient in products”.
Trump is showing the Europeans “he doesn’t want to deal with Europe and to hell with them … This is opening the rift between the US and the EU further,” said Stambolis.
(Al Jazeera) Ukraine says it has destroyed roughly half of Russia’s refining capacity, forcing Moscow to stop exporting lucrative petroleum products which help it to finance its war.
It has also bombed Russian tankers carrying crude oil to global markets.
Zelenskyy said the strategy was effective, and Trump’s deal, which would suspend sanctions on Russian oil products until April 2027, undermined it.
“Gifts to Putin will not lead to peace,” Zelenskyy said Saturday. “Any weakening of sanctions against Russia without a clear and lasting de-escalation agreement with Russia is an obvious sign of weakness.”
Although Trump announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on Sunday, leading Ukraine to suspend its attacks on refineries, Russian strikes pounded Kyiv’s energy grid and killed 12 people in Dnipropetrovsk.
“I do not think he has earned a respite,” Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said of Zelenskyy.
Europe supports Ukraine’s economic strategy against Russia’s war machine, but Trump has blamed it for raising petrol prices at the pump for Americans as he heads into Congressional midterm elections in early November.
“[Zelenskyy] wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel because Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel throughout the world,” Trump told reporters in the White House after Zelenskyy’s reaction.
“I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president ,” he said.
Trump has followed a seemingly self-contradictory policy towards Russia.
He cut US military aid to Ukraine when he assumed power in January 2025, but agreed to sell Europe weapons to help Ukraine.
He had a public dispute with Zelenskyy in the Oval Office in February 2025, saying “You don’t have the cards,” but at the NATO summit this year said Zelenskyy had “done an amazing job” and “been very effective”.
Last month, Trump signed the Lindsey Graham Act, which would allow him to punish countries buying Russian oil. Eleven days later, he reversed policy.
“The moment the pendulum comes to one side, Trump tries to balance it with a completely different and opposite tool,” said Victoria Vdovychenko, an expert on European security at Cambridge University’s Centre for Geopolitics.
“In this way he sees how he controls the narrative, but also negotiations of any kind,” she told Al Jazeera. “So this pendulum will continue to prevail.”
According to the US Energy Information Agency (EIA), average US diesel and petrol prices briefly spiked but ultimately changed little on account of the Ukraine war, yet they have risen a great deal on account of the US-Israel war on Iran.
US diesel was priced at $4.10 a gallon on the day of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, February 24, 2022. It had fallen to $3.81 on the eve of Trump’s Gulf war, February 28, 2026.
A worker fills his truck with diesel fuel at a corporate filling station in San Diego, California, US, May 18, 2026 [Mike Blake/Reuters] It has since risen by 78 percent, to $6.19 in early October.
It is a similar story for US regular unleaded gasoline, priced at $3.48 a gallon before the Russian invasion. It stood at $2.79 before Trump’s Gulf war, but has since risen by half, to $4.15 a gallon.
The US government has little room to reduce taxes, which constitute just 11 or 12 percent of retail price, so it can only manipulate prices through supply.
“If the market knows that there will be much more diesel in the coming weeks, it factors this into today’s prices and discounts it now,” Stambolis told Al Jazeera.
But much more important in bringing down oil prices than the Trump-Putin deal will be an October 2 announcement by the G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil from strategic reserves, he said.
A remainder of 80 million barrels from a previous, 400-million-tonne release in March will also be released.
“This release will start happening in the next two weeks,” Stambolis said. “The world is 5 million barrels a day short of crude compared to before the Gulf war. It’s a very significant percentage on 100 million. All prices vary on this margin.”

items.title: Iran may be digging in for next war, raising stakes for US, Israel, and Gulf - The Jerusalem Post
items.summary: Iran may be digging in for next war, raising stakes for US, Israel, and Gulf  The Jerusalem Post
items.content:
Iran fortifies nuclear sites, rebuilds missile arsenal as it prepares for the next war - analysis
The emerging picture is of an Iran continuing its efforts to rebuild its missile and drone programs despite the damage inflicted by previous US and Israeli strikes.
Smoke and flames rise at the site of airstrikes on an oil depot in Tehran on March 7, 2026.
( photo credit : Sasan / Middle East Images / AFP via Getty Images )
Satellite images show that Iran is fortifying various locations as it may be preparing for renewed war, The Wall Street Journal reported on Monday.
“Iran is fortifying its defenses, rallying loyalists and threatening a wider, harsher response against the US and its Gulf allies as it prepares for potential American attacks after the midterms and seeks to deter them,” the article noted.
This comes amid a flurry of other reports suggesting that the US or Israel could return to fighting Iran.
Maariv said over the weekend that the United States had pressured Israel to carry out strikes against Iran. Both Israel and the US have upcoming elections. Any strikes could affect the elections.
PBS reported on Sunday that “Iran has continued to reject a deal with the US. The head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council says Tehran finds the latest response from the United States ‘insufficient’ as efforts at negotiations to end the war and fully open the Strait of Hormuz limp along.”
Smoke rises following an explosion, after Israel's Defence Minister Israel Katz said Israel had launched a pre-emptive attack against Iran, in Tehran, Iran February 28, 2026 in this screen grab taken from video. (credit: WANA (WEST ASIA NEWS AGENCY) VIA REUTERS)
The picture being painted is of an Iran that continues attempting to rebuild its missile and drone program.
Netanyahu said Iran can no longer produce ballistic missiles
In March, Israel’s prime minister said that the Islamic Republic could no longer produce ballistic missiles due to its hammering by US and Israeli strikes. There was also an optimistic assessment about how many Iranian launchers had been destroyed and how many missiles were “corked” in their depots by collapsing routes to the missiles.
In April, The New York Times reported that Iran was repairing its missile bunkers. The regime has shown it can rebuild capabilities.
The WSJ report noted that “Iran has also reinforced protection around its nuclear sites and other security-related bunkers. Last month, it built passive defense measures such as makeshift dirt mounds around its Pickaxe Mountain and Natanz nuclear sites to impede any attempted raid by ground forces, according to Vantor satellite images analyzed by the Institute for Science and International Security, a Washington, DC, nonprofit.”
The report quoted Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies. “In both word and deed, the Islamic Republic is actively preparing for the next war,” Ben Taleblu said.
Iran is a huge country, around 75 times the size of Israel and 150 times the size of Lebanon. Israel has struggled to defeat Hezbollah in Lebanon and remove all its threats. This illustrates the challenge of locating all the Iranian threats. The new report at the WSJ is concerning in this respect.
“Satellite images show Iran is strengthening sensitive locations, including nuclear sites and border areas, to make them more resilient to attacks. The government is also preparing Iranians for renewed war, sending paramilitary forces to read war stories to kindergartners, advertising training in firing shoulder-mounted anti-aircraft missiles, and holding rallies,” the report added.
It also said that Iran is prepared to defend against various types of airstrikes. It has likely learned some lessons from the 12 Day War in June 2025, as well as the round of strikes that began in February 2026 and lasted until May.
Iran continues to threaten shipping via the Strait of Hormuz . The US has been working to make sure that ships can pass the Strait. It is trying to make sure that the crisis with Iran doesn’t affect energy prices too much. However, all the levers the US has tried to pull still leave the conflict with Iran as an open-ended problem.
The WSJ noted that “Iranian officials have hinted that their forces could conduct land incursions into neighboring countries, according to people familiar with the warnings.”
With US forces having withdrawn from Iraq on September 30, this could give Iran some opportunities. It could try to infiltrate via Iraq or use Iranian-backed militias in Iraq to conduct more attacks. Those militias have already attacked a key pipeline in Saudi Arabia.
While US Central Command (CENTCOM) and Saudi Arabia carried out retaliatory strikes in July, there is reticence in Riyadh to confront the militias in Iraq and the Houthis at the same time.
A plume of smoke rises during a reported airstrike by the Saudi-led coalition on the Houthi-controlled Yemeni capital Sana'a, October 9, 2026 (credit: AFP via Getty Images)
This is why the WSJ report is important. It notes that “Tehran has separately warned Arab officials that it could strike regional targets, including Saudi oil facilities, in the event of a renewed conflict, some of the people said.”
Saudi Arabia is already weighing how to deal with the Houthi threat, which has targeted Saudi airports in recent days, killing and wounding people.
The question now is whether a return to fighting by the US or Israel will lead to better results than in the past.
Iran is seeking to rebuild; this means increasing its drone arsenal as well. The regime has had some success in attacking US bases in the region . It can read the same media reports as everyone else about how those attacks damaged facilities and airplanes and caused the US to reposition assets.
The one email that makes sense of the Middle East. Iran, the Gulf, Syria, Turkey, and whatever moved that day, from The Jerusalem Post, every evening.

items.title: Germany shifts toward tougher EU trade defenses as pressure from Chinese competition grows - dw.com
items.summary: <a href="https://news.google.
items.content:
Germany and France are pushing for stronger EU trade defense tools amid rising Chinese competition Image: DW Advertisement
Germany's cautious approach toward Beijing is cracking. For years, Berlin blocked a harder line on what the European Union describes as China's   unfair trade practices.
In the last few months, that caution — a fear of Chinese retaliation that could hurt  German exporters — has given way to a willingness to escalate.
Last week, Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron wrote jointly to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen seeking a new tool to cut a trading partner off from the EU's single market  if unfair practices continue.
Clearly aimed at Beijing, the letter warned the measure was necessary against countries that "deliberately seek to undermine ... fair market conditions by political or economic means." 
China's Commerce Ministry warned Europe would "suffer the consequences" if it adopted such a "kill-switch" plan, which was timed to coincide with crucial EU-China trade talks in Beijing last week.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Noah Barkin, a senior adviser with research consultancy Rhodium Group's China practice, told DW that the threats to Germany's export powerhouse "have convinced Merz and his closest advisers that the benefits of action outweigh the costs of inaction." 
Before the COVID pandemic , the two economies rose in tandem and German industry benefited from China's ascent .
Since 2021, however, China has fallen from Germany's second-largest export market to its ninth, according to data from Germany Trade & Invest for the first half of 2026.
Chinese competitors have quickly closed the technology gap and benefit from much lower costs and state subsidies. That pressure is being felt especially in Germany's automaking , precision engineering and chemicals industries.
German vehicle makers have suffered a large sales drop in China, which was once their second-largest market. According to data from Rhodium Group, German car exports to China plummeted by 66% between 2022 and 2025.
Big German brands now face heavy rivalry from a new wave of Chinese electric vehicle (EV) manufactures in other major markets, including Europe, which is forcing a wave of  layoffs and possible factory closures .
VW, Audi and Porsche have announced workforce reductions totaling tens of thousands of jobs as the industry undergoes a huge transformation Image: Sven Hoppe/dpa/picture alliance
In Germany alone, imports of new Chinese-made cars rose 121% in the first seven months of the year, according to Destatis, the federal statistics agency. Overall, Chinese-made vehicles accounted for nearly 14% of total vehicle imports.
"After continuously losing market share in China ... it [the rivalry] seems to be hitting their business within the European automotive market," Andreas Mischer, an associate fellow at the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies (MERICS), told DW.
Mischer said pressure from Germany's powerful automotive lobby was key to Berlin's "shifting attitude toward trade defense instruments."
Among the many German business leaders who have demanded a more hard-line approach in recent months, Oliver Richtberg, head of foreign trade at VDMA, Germany's mechanical engineering association, was perhaps the most blunt:
"We are currently being deindustrialized through unfair measures — and most companies are no longer willing to accept this," Richtberg told Welt am Sonntag newspaper in August.
According to Eurostat, the wider EU's goods deficit with China was around €360 billion ($402 billion) last year — effectively €1 billion per day — and widened again in the first half of 2026.
While Brussels has been pushing back against the dumping of cheap Chinese goods, a separate industrial protection law and other anti-coercion measures are running into trouble from Beijing and at home.
Business groups question industrial policy proposals
The EU's Industrial Accelerator Act, proposed in March, aims to pull manufacturing investment back to Europe by favoring EU-based firms in public contracts and subsidies.
Foreign investments in key sectors would only be approved if European partners keep majority control, which Beijing has framed as discriminatory.
How to dismantle China's stranglehold on raw materials?
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) warned last month that the draft act does little to counter the threat from cheaper Chinese rivals. In a position paper, it said the incentive to produce within the bloc has to be large enough to "cancel out the extra cost of producing locally."
Berlin's chief concern was that China could place new export curbs on rare earth minerals and the magnets made from them. China has a stranglehold on these elements, which are essential for German automotive, renewables and defense manufacturing.
Bloomberg last week cited unnamed German officials as saying that a new EU kill-switch could be a "second-strike weapon" if Beijing blocked those exports. Brussels is also considering unilateral limits on how many hybrid cars China can export to the EU, according to the same Bloomberg report. 
Perhaps to avoid such an open confrontation, the EU and China reached a "shared understanding" last week at the EU-China trade talks in Beijing that could cut Chinese exports of hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles to the European Union by more than half, according to EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic, who headed the European delegation.
Reports say the agreement would cap such Chinese imports at 350,000 vehicles annually, with the limit increasing by 6% each year over four years.
Amid intense Chinese rivalry, the EU says it wants to restore industrial production in Europe Image: Torsten Krüger/imageBROKER/picture alliance Overall, new hybrid-electric cars in the EU reached nearly 37% of all new cars registered from January to August, according to ACEA data.
MERICS, meanwhile, calculated that the EU is a more critical export market for China than the US. In the first half of the year, Chinese exports to the EU were $254 billion (€354 billion), versus $172 billion to the US.
This could give EU negotiators a firmer hand as they seek to avoid a trade war while protecting Europe from China's latest export glut.
"The EU has more leverage than it sometimes thinks," MERICS' Mischer told DW.

items.content:
A Russian fuel oil terminal in the Black Sea port of Novorossiisk. Moscow says the country’s diesel exports could return to previous levels by the end of the year in the wake of the fuel deal with Donald Trump. Photograph: Reuters
A Russian fuel oil terminal in the Black Sea port of Novorossiisk. Moscow says the country’s diesel exports could return to previous levels by the end of the year in the wake of the fuel deal with Donald Trump. Photograph: Reuters
Ukraine war briefing: Russian diesel exports could return to past levels after Trump deal, Moscow claims
Exports could reach 3.5m metric tons a month, deputy PM says, after collapsing amid Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries. What we know on day 1,693
Russia will be able to return its diesel exports to levels not seen since Ukraine started to target the country’s oil refineries, deputy prime minister Alexander Novak has claimed, after the Trump administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian ⁠fuel. Russia has seen diesel exports collapse ⁠due to ​Ukraine’s attacks on oil refineries and it self-imposed overseas sales restrictions. Trump announced on Friday that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets in order to ease supply concerns, in a deal that has drawn condemnation from Ukraine and other US allies. Novak said on the Rossiya-24 state TV channel on Monday: “We will see how ‌the situation develops further, ‌but Russia has the capacity to increase diesel fuel exports. By the end of the year, exports could reach 3-3.5m metric tons per month, returning to the levels seen before the crisis.”
The diesel deal, under which Russia will supply more than 2.25m barrels of diesel to US and global markets, has triggered a bipartisan backlash from some US lawmakers , who say it will give Moscow cash to pursue its war without forcing Putin to make concessions to end the conflict. A group ‌of Republican and Democratic US senators called on Trump to “reverse course” on the deal, saying it might violate a 2022 law designed to support Ukraine in its bid to repel Russian invaders. “We should be tightening sanctions further, not undercutting them…,” Republican senator Jerry Moran said on social media. But Trump defended the deal on Monday, calling it “the right choice for the American people”.
Trump’s envoys have told Ukrainian officials that the deal to allow Russian diesel exports is part of a bid to draw Moscow back to negotiations , Reuters has quoted three people familiar with the meeting as saying . Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner told ⁠the Ukrainians in a meeting in Miami on Friday that ​Russian president Vladimir Putin was not prepared to negotiate an end to his war in Ukraine and that the diesel deal announced last week could help restart trilateral talks, said two of the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity. The third person said the US relayed to the Ukrainians that the deal could help “soften” Moscow’s position ⁠in part because it “sends a signal that Trump is open to do things” with Russia. The report has not been officially confirmed.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy vowed to respond to Russia’s continuing attacks on the Ukrainian power grid as European leaders rallied around Kyiv amid a feud with Trump over Ukraine’s strikes on oil refineries. The Ukrainian president told a gathering of European security officials in Warsaw on Monday that Kyiv would retaliate if strikes on its power grid continued. “If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire this winter, we will respond.” Zelenskyy later told Fox News his government had refrained from striking Russian energy sites since Trump’s truce announcement on Sunday, and was ready to honour an energy ceasefire as “a good first step” toward closing the war.
⁠A Russian strike on a high-rise residential building in a suburb of Kyiv killed two people ⁠and ​injured at least nine, while attacks in other Ukrainian regions killed at least six people , officials said ⁠on Monday. Two people died in the evening strike on the 25-storey ⁠residence in the Ukrainian capital’s Darnitskyi district, Zelenskyy said on Telegram. In Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-largest city, mayor Ihor Terekhov reported serious shelling of city districts, with five people injured in the collapse of an entrance to an apartment building. Residents ‌of the north-eastern city could still be trapped beneath rubble, he said.
The EU will on Tuesday open new negotiations with Ukraine , an essential step in Kyiv’s long path to join the bloc. Ukrainian legislators on Monday passed legislation protecting the rights of national minorities, which removes a major hurdle in Kyiv’s bid for membership. European Council president António Costa said he welcomed “today’s decision by EU member states to open two further negotiation clusters with Ukraine and Moldova”. “Your future lies in the EU,” he said. “Let’s keep up the momentum!”

items.title: Microsoft Now Has 3 Generations of Its Own AI Chips. Nvidia Is Still the Chip Stock to Buy. - Yahoo Finance
items.summary: Microsoft Now Has 3 Generations of Its Own AI Chips. Nvidia Is Still the Chip Stock to Buy.  Yahoo Finance
items.content:
Microsoft Now Has 3 Generations of Its Own AI Chips. Nvidia Is Still the Chip Stock to Buy.
Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) now has a third generation of its own artificial intelligence (AI) chip. The tech giant announced Maia 300 on Monday and said it will ramp up its Maia chips starting in 2027 to make them the main system running AI in its own products.
That might sound like trouble for Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA). The AI chip leader gets around half its revenue from big cloud companies like Microsoft, a group it calls hyperscale customers.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
But I don't think the news matters much for Nvidia shares. The company's quarterly revenue is over five times what it was right before Microsoft's first Maia chip launched in late 2023. And Microsoft still buys Nvidia's chips.
In the announcement, Microsoft said it will make Maia "the primary inference system for Microsoft products and services." Inference means using an AI model once it's been trained.
Microsoft also said it expects Maia 300 to generate 40% more tokens (units of AI output) per megawatt than top systems built around graphics processing units , the type of chip Nvidia sells. Still, that's Microsoft's own estimate for a chip that isn't set to start production deployments until 2027.
Meanwhile, CEO Satya Nadella said on Microsoft's July earnings call that the company will be one of the first cloud providers to deploy Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin systems. Management guided for capital expenditures of over $50 billion in the quarter that ended in September.
That would be up from $41 billion in Microsoft's fiscal fourth quarter of 2026 (the period ended June 30, 2026), which was itself up from $24.2 billion a year before. Around two-thirds of that quarter's spending went toward shorter-lived assets, mostly chips.
The first Maia chip launched in November 2023, and Maia 200 followed in January 2026. In the quarter ending right before the first one came out, Nvidia's fiscal third quarter of 2024 (the period ended Oct. 29, 2023), revenue was $18.1 billion.
Showing how little in-house chips have slowed Nvidia since then, the company took in $96.2 billion in the fiscal second quarter of 2027 (the period ended July 26, 2026). That was up 106% year over year -- faster than the 85% growth in fiscal Q1. Earnings per share jumped 128%. What's more, hyperscale customers, the ones with the most reason to buy fewer Nvidia chips, more than doubled their spending to $48.7 billion.
Nvidia's fiscal Q3 guidance of around $108 billion points to growth of about 89%. And for fiscal 2028, chief financial officer Colette Kress said on the August earnings call that the company expects revenue to rise about 70% -- a forecast she described as held back by supply. Fiscal 2028 includes most of 2027, the year Microsoft plans to start ramping Maia up.
True, Amazon and Alphabet design their own AI chips, too. And Nvidia's sales are concentrated, with one direct customer making up 16% of revenue in fiscal Q2. If its top buyers shifted most of their AI work to their own chips, Nvidia's growth could slow quickly.
But Nvidia's sales outside the hyperscale group are growing even faster. Revenue from its other data center customers (AI cloud providers, businesses, and governments) climbed 138% year over year to $40.3 billion. Hyperscale customers' share of data center revenue dropped from around 59% a year earlier to about 55%.
On Nvidia's August earnings call, CEO Jensen Huang described many custom chips as "inference-specific chips for one cloud or one service." He called Nvidia's product "an entire AI factory platform that spans the entire AI life cycle that you can use in any cloud."
I'd say Maia matches his description. Microsoft built it to power Microsoft's products.
In the end, custom chips like Maia might take some work from Nvidia. But the stock arguably isn't priced as if Nvidia will keep all of it.
Shares trade near $226 as of this writing, about 6% off the record close they set on Oct. 6. That price is about 14 times what analysts expect Nvidia to earn on average in fiscal 2028 (the 12 months through January 2028). For Microsoft's fiscal 2028 (ending June 2028), the same number is about 23 times earnings.
I think Nvidia's price is cheap for a company still guiding for growth around 90%. It remains the chip stock I'd consider buying now.

items.title: S&P 500 is flat after bank earnings deluge; Nasdaq slides on chip stock weakness: Live updates - CNBC
items.summary: S&P 500 is flat after bank earnings deluge; Nasdaq slides on chip stock weakness: Liv
items.content:
Traders work at the New York Stock Exchange on June 26, 2026.
Stocks were mixed on Tuesday, with traders digesting a slew of corporate earnings reports from major banks along with a steep overnight decline in South Korea that put pressure on memory names.
The S&P 500 was down 0.1%, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 0.3%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average outperformed, rising 359 points, or 0.7%.
JPMorgan Chase reported third-quarter earnings and revenue that missed analyst expectations. The stock initially fell on the weaker-than-expected results, but it later recovered to trade 2% higher after the bank raised its net interest income guidance for 2026. Wells Fargo shed nearly 1% on mixed Q3 numbers, while Goldman Sachs jumped 2% after its revenue for the third quarter surpassed expectations.
UnitedHealth , meanwhile, rose 3% after the insurance giant's results exceeded analyst expectations.
Memory stocks were under pressure after South Korea's Kospi benchmark dropped 5.5% — reaching its lowest level since July 31 — on valuation concerns in the space along with growing competition out of China. This week, China's CXMT said it plans to release a new, more powerful chip by year-end.
SK hynix , along with Seagate Technology , dropped around 6%, while Western Digital lost 7%. Micron Technology and Sandisk fell more than 5% and more than 4%, respectively.
The early reports could set the tone for an earnings season with lofty expectations. Analysts on average expect S&P 500 profits grew by nearly 30% from the year-earlier period, according to FactSet.
"Three groups will likely shape how investors read the season: 1) Banks (consumer and business health), 2) Big Tech (AI monetization), and 3) Energy (the durability of oil-driven profits)," wrote Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at Ameriprise. "Underneath these areas, the health of consumers and businesses amid higher interest rates, elevated costs, and concerns about the macroeconomic environment will be closely monitored across sectors throughout the season."
Investors on Tuesday will also parse through existing home sales figures along with commentary from Federal Reserve officials Tom Barkin and Susan Collins.
Later in the week, inflation data for September will be released – which could jolt Treasury yields after they reached multidecade highs recently. The U.S. bond market was closed Monday due to the Indigenous Peoples' Day holiday.
Piper Sandler upgrades VF Corp to overweight from neutral
Piper Sandler upgraded VF Corp  to overweight from neutral on Tuesday.
Piper Sandler's Fall Teen Survey of about 9,000 respondents found Vans ranked as a top footwear for male consumers.
"As a favorite footwear brand for all males (vast majority of customer base), Vans maintained its #7 spot vs. declining the past three surveys; for upper income guy, the brand moved up one spot," analyst Anna Andreeva wrote in a note to clients.
Vans web traffic performance for the fiscal second quarter of 2027 was strong while foot traffic signaled to be positive, she said. Andreeva also raised her target to $20 from $16, implying 26.7% upside from Monday's close.
Investor Paul Tudor Jones delivers a bearish roar on the market
Paul Tudor Jones, founder and chief investment officer of Tudor Investment, speaks with CNBC's Squawk Box on Oct. 13th, 2026.
Famous investor Paul Tudor Jones delivered some bearish pronouncements on market conditions in a Tuesday interview on CNBC's " Squawk Box ."
He compared current conditions to the period just before the dot com bubble popped in the early 2000s, tracing the similarities to increasingly debt-financed capital investments powering the artificial intelligence buildout and global sovereign debt levels.
He said that 2027 is going to be a very challenging year for the stock market and that he'll be short for the duration. He also sees oil prices rising between $20 and $25 dollars from their current levels.
"I'll be short the whole year. There just -- there's little value," Jones said. "You had all this issuance, all these IPOs in 98 and 99, and really 2000, 2001, 2002. Those were the easiest years to be short because you kept having these unlocks that just kept adding supply to the market."
Jones added that he expects another federal bailout to follow the crash he is anticipating.
"We're never going to fix these deficits until the market makes us to. It's going to be just like 2008 and TARP [Troubled Asset Relief Program]. So that's the reality. items.title: The Strait of Hormuz Crisis is the Vulnerability Accelerator for Southeast Asia’s Energy System - Energy for Growth Hub
items.summary: The Strait of Hormuz Crisis is the Vulnerability Accelerator for Southeast Asia’s Energy System  Energy for Growth Hu
items.content:
Strategic Vulnerabilities Translate into Price Shocks
Southeast Asia is structurally vulnerable to geopolitical energy shocks. Since 2010, fossil fuels have met nearly 80% of the region’s rapidly growing energy demand . Although some countries in the region produce oil and gas, they are not entirely self-sufficient (see Table 1). For others that rely heavily on imports, supply shocks hit harder. Unlike East Asian countries, most Southeast Asian countries have very limited strategic stockpiles as a buffer.
The oil and gas price hike is an immediate fiscal burden for Southeast Asian countries. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) estimated that monthly import costs would increase by $3.36 billion . Because oil and gas account for 90% of the transportation sector and 31% of the electricity sector's needs in the region, price shocks have rippled through society, translating into higher estimated inflation across countries.
Governments Respond with Conservation and Subsidies
Countries soon rolled out extreme energy-conservation measures, but only for the public sector. They cut workdays, canceled travel, and limited air-conditioning in government buildings (See Table 2). These measures aimed to reduce demand among civil servants and encourage the public to change their behavior. However, governments didn’t impose large-scale rationing for industries or households for fear of political turmoil .
Many governments are doubling down on fossil fuel subsidies. Before the crisis, Indonesia, Malaysia, Viet Nam, Thailand, and the Philippines directly subsidized fossil fuels to lower prices, reaching $54.2 billion in total subsidies in 2024 and accounting for significant shares of each country’s GDP (see Table 3). After the crisis, Indonesia announced an additional $28.4 billion to fund fossil fuel subsidies and compensate state-owned energy and utility companies. Subsidies also jumped sevenfold in Malaysia and will reach $9.8 billion in 2026, which is 9.5% of the annual budget.
Crisis Mitigation Efforts Could Hamper Power Systems Long-Term
A crowding-out effect will undermine governments’ abilities to pursue other priorities. According to Indonesia’s Minister of Finance , the new fossil fuel subsidies will come from “spending cuts at ​some government agencies.” The response pattern follows what these governments did in 2022, when energy prices rose following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. In Indonesia, energy subsidies in 2022 accounted for 2.8% of the GDP, exceeding government expenditure on education, social protection, health, and economic affairs.
Governments must strengthen the power system while navigating energy shocks. Southeast Asia's grid has long faced challenges from a varied landscape, frequent natural disasters, densely concentrated urban demand, and growing intermittent renewables. Southeast Asia needs to more than double its grid capacity to meet projected demand by 2050. Doing so will require investing 14 times the amount invested since the 1970s, especially as countries focus on job-creating, energy-intensive sectors. The grid’s inability to keep up with industrial demand can create multiple problems. For example, the rapid expansion of nickel processing has driven up the construction of off-grid/captive coal generation in Indonesia.
1. How to supply electricity at manageable costs while keeping up with demand growth?
Industrial plans mean further surges in electricity demand. Indonesia, Malaysia, Viet Nam, Thailand, and the Philippines have industrial policies that require large amounts of electricity. They hope to expand data centers, mineral processing, semiconductor manufacturing, and electric vehicle manufacturing. According to the International Energy Agency, this means that the region’s electricity demand will grow by 4.4% annually to 2035 and more than double by 2050.
With ongoing uncertainty in the international energy market, these governments will have to figure out how to leverage supply- and demand-side policy tools to mitigate shocks while keeping up with a growing thirst for energy.
2. How to manage demand without further straining the power systems?
A surge in demand strains the grid, especially where capacity is limited. A month-long on-and-off blackout in Northern Viet Nam in 2024 cost the country $1.4 billion , equivalent to 0.3% of its GDP. Data centers, which demand intensive and stable electricity, can have sharp ramp-up and ramp-down profiles and pose new forecasting challenges and outage risks for system operators. Industries the region actively seeks to develop, including electric vehicles, semiconductors, and other types of advanced manufacturing, are also highly sensitive to power outages.
The region has to figure out how to bridge the persistent investment gap in new grid infrastructure and manage existing grid vulnerabilities in order to pursue economic growth driven by electricity-intensive industrial users.
Conclusion: Southeast Asia’s Future Growth Depends on Energy
The crisis response measures Southeast Asian countries rolled out are unsustainable. They drain governments’ ability to manage other priorities, including industrial growth. To meet their growth and development priorities, governments need a multi-pronged energy security strategy that plans for supply shocks while investing in energy infrastructure. Without this dual approach, both industries and consumers will continue to suffer from price hikes, unstable supply, and limited investment due to the fiscal pressures facing these governments.

Qnity (Q), a key supplier of semiconductor materials to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSM) and Intel (INTC), is reportedly betting that local production and sourcing will help it win more business from chipmakers.
The strategy comes amid rising demand for materials used throughout the AI chip supply chain, including in technologies developed by Nvidia (NVDA).

CEO Jon Kemp told Nikkei Asia Qnity's "local-for-local" strategy, which involves sourcing more than 70% of its raw materials within the regions where it operates, helps the company respond faster to customers, strengthen supply chains, and win a role in developing advanced chip technologies.
"Our belief in that local-for-local operating model and being that partner of choice is to allow us to accelerate the pace of innovation and match the speed of our customers," Kemp said.
Q stock edged as much as 1% lower in pre-market trade, on track to extend a drop of over 6% over the past five days. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around Qnity slipped to 'bearish' from 'neutral' territory over the past day.
Qnity's strategy reflects a broader shift in the semiconductor industry, the report said.
Tariffs, industrial policy and concern about production concentrated in Taiwan are pushing chipmakers and suppliers to build closer to customers.
The U.S. imposed Section 232 chip tariffs in January and signed a reshoring deal with Taiwan the following day. TSMC is expanding in Arizona, and GlobalFoundries last week agreed to make interposers for TSMC in New York.
For Qnity, Kemp said the company's manufacturing footprint and regional sourcing model give it an advantage by improving supply chain resilience, creating new business opportunities, and reducing exposure to logistics-driven inflation.
Qnity recently invested $61.5 million to expand production capacity for advanced semiconductor materials and chemicals in Taiwan. It is also expanding in South Korea and has doubled its capacity in Vietnam.
In the U.S., the company opened a facility in Delaware earlier this year to support growing domestic production of advanced processors and memory chips.
Qnity supplies semiconductor chemicals and materials to major chipmakers, including TSMC, Samsung and Intel. Its portfolio includes chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) pads and slurries, plus materials for advanced chip packaging and thermal management.
Kemp said Qnity's CMP-related business grew 20% in 2026. Materials for advanced packaging, AI-related printed circuit boards and thermal management applications each grew more than 50% year over year in the first half of the year.
"Materials are moving kind of from backstage to center stage," Kemp said. "Materials innovation is a hidden hero of the AI era."
In pre-market trade, TSM stock fell nearly 1% while INTC stock was down as much as 1.5%. Meanwhile, NVDA stock shed more than 1% amid broader weakness in semiconductor stocks. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around NVDA and INTC continued to trend in 'bearish' territory over the past day. Sentiment around TSM deteriorated to 'neutral' from the 'bullish' zone.
Qnity is scheduled to report its third-quarter (Q3) earnings results on November 4. Investors will be watching whether growth converts to free cash flow under incoming CFO Ken Rizvi. The company guided to $600 million to $700 million in free cash flow this year.

The new technology from Microsoft is part of its plan to ease its reliance on chips developed by Nvidia. Azure Maia 300 represents the launch of the company's third-generation of AI accelerator technology.
Maia 300 builds on the architecture of Maia 200, which marked a new step in AI accelerators with the introduction of Software Defined Locally Accessed Dataflow Architecture.
"Maia 300 brings 2.5 times the memory bandwidth, 33% more capacity, and approximately 2 times the HBM bandwidth per watt compared with Maia 200," Microsoft said in its announcement.
Microsoft has relied on Nvidia's GPU technology, as have many industry leaders. Nvidia's GPU is used in data centers and AI model training for OpenAI and Anthropic as well.
Microsoft will begin production on Maia 300 units in 2027. The company intends to place 96 Maia 300 chips into each of its data center racks, about twice as much as the Maia 200 chips.
Microsoft is not yet completely abandoning Nvidia technology. In its announcement of its new line of Microsoft Surface laptops, its specs include Nvidia processing power. Microsoft also works with technology by AMD.

items.title: Fridges in French supermarkets hit by cyber attack
items.summary: Hundreds of stores were targeted by the overnight hack, which spoiled fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.
items.content:
By Ian Aikman Â  and Â  Hugh Schofield ,Â  Paris correspondent
Hundreds of French supermarkets have been hit by a cyber attack that caused their fridges and freezers to heat up, spoiling fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.
Hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units, forcing some to warm to 50C (120F) overnight, according to one supermarket chain affected.
The chief executive of CoopÃ©rative U said several of its supermarkets had been hit by the "extremely serious and unprecedented" attack.
More than 100 of the chain's supermarkets were targeted, while 180 stores from IntermarchÃ© and its Netto brand were affected, with a spokesman saying that another 100 shops were urgently disconnected from the internet to prevent the same thing happening to them.
Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss.
The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely.
Normally, supermarket freezers go through a short period of defrosting overnight, in which temperatures rise slightly. But the hackers ordered the units to heat up and stay hot, although Danfoss did not confirm any reports about just how warm the fridges and freezers could become in that process.
Danfoss said the affected cold units were older models whose security software could not be updated to ward off a risk they had identified.
The firm added in a statement that it had "long advised" businesses to keep supported systems up to date.
"Reliable refrigeration is critical to our customers' operations, and we remain committed to supporting our customers and helping them maintain secure and reliable systems they are used to."
The full scale of the attack is unclear, but figures supplied by individual chains suggest about 400 stores were affected out of 15,000 or so overall in France.
Carrefour said fridges in 80 of its 6,000 stores were hacked, while Monoprix said 5% of its 400-plus stores had been hit, with food removed from sale if its condition could not be guaranteed.
In a statement to the BBC, Mousquetaires Group - which owns IntermarchÃ© and Netto - said some fresh and frozen food display units remained out of service on Monday afternoon.
The stores had "taken all necessary precautions to remove the products from these units", it said, adding that staff were working to restock the shelves "as soon as possible".
IntermarchÃ© said its fridges had heated up to 50C for six hours overnight into Monday, and the retailer had thrown away all the affected food to avoid health risks, the Reuters news agency reported.
As a result of the attack, managers arriving at branches of several supermarket chains on Monday morning were hit by a wave of hot air from the freezers. In some places there were even small fires.
French broadcaster BFMTV published an image showing a freezer in an ice cream aisle displaying a temperature of 26.5C.
Two supermarkets in the Alsace region reported losses of â¬270,000 (Â£228,000) between them, the broadcaster added, meaning the nationwide total could run into the millions.
French prosecutors have opened a specific cyber-crime investigation into the incident, which the Paris prosecutor's office called a "large-scale cyber-attack affecting the refrigerators of several major food retail chains across France".
European Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen condemned the hack in a post on X and added: "Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponisation of food has become a reality."
In a post on X, CoopÃ©rative chief executive Dominique Schelcher said staff were "fully mobilised, in co-ordination with refrigeration specialists, to restore the situation as quickly as possible".
He called for an investigation into the hack and said targeting equipment essential to the French food supply was "unacceptable".

Britain has appealed to Interpol to reject Argentina’s requests for the arrest of individuals involved in a large oil project off the Falkland Islands .
With tensions over the sovereignty of the British overseas territory reaching levels not seen since the war with Argentina in 1982, UK officials have sought urgent assurances from the international organisation.
A letter has been sent to Interpol’s headquarters in Lyon arguing that “red notice” requests from Argentina for the arrest of such individuals, including British nationals, should be seen as politically motivated.
It is understood that the UK government is concerned by what sources suggested was an attempt to bully people and companies out of working in the Falklands .
The chief executive of the Falkland Islands, Dr Andrea Clausen, in the room where Argentinian forces surrendered. Photograph: Sean Smith/The Guardian An oil project known as Sea Lion in the north Falklands basin in the south Atlantic has the potential to triple the Falklands’ GDP but Argentina’s president, Javier Milei , has vowed to block it. Argentina’s strategy includes attempts to criminalise those involved in Sea Lion and deter other investors.
In its letter, the UK government has urged Interpol to be cautious in its handling of Argentinian requests for detentions, it is understood.
Andrea Clausen, the chief executive of the Falklands government, confirmed that the use of Interpol by Argentina was a threat but added: “One would hope that Interpol wouldn’t necessarily take action.”
She said: “Certainly those of us who have an interest have had a look at certain sections of Interpol’s constitution to see what we think it could mean.”
It is understood that a response from Interpol to the UK government’s correspondence stated that it would respect article 3 of its constitution, which forbids it from undertaking any intervention or activities of a political character.
Interpol screens red notices, which are requests to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition. If circulated to the enforcement agencies, individual member countries then decide whether to act on the requests. Nearly 20,000 were issued last year.
The Foreign Office has been approached for comment.
The intensity of the Argentinian menace relating to the Falklands is at a level that UK officials say has not been seen since the war 44 years ago that followed the invasion ordered by Argentina’s dictator Gen Leopoldo Galtieri.
The 74-day conflict ended with the surrender of the Argentinian forces and cost the lives of 649 of its military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland islanders.
Argentina continues to claim sovereignty over the 700 islands that make up the Falklands and has dismissed a 2013 referendum in which 99.8% of the islands’ 3,600 residents voted to remain a British territory, with only three votes against .
Despite Interpol’s reassurance about its screening of red notice requests, concerns remain that Argentina could convince the organisation’s member states that its requests are not political but rooted in domestic legislation.
Milei has initiated criminal proceedings against the Israeli company Navitas and its British partner, Rockhopper Exploration, which are the core companies in the offshore Sea Lion project.
A draft national sovereignty introduced to Argentina’s congress would further expand the scope of sanctions to affiliates of those companies, financial intermediaries, shareholders and suppliers.
The bill additionally contains clauses that could target those involved in the fishing industry in the Falklands, which makes up a large part of the islands’ economy. The archipelago is 300 miles (500km) east of the southern Patagonian coast of Argentina.
Workers in the oil and fisheries sectors on the Falklands – known in Argentina as Las Malvinas – are understood to be concerned that they could be targeted should they travel, particularly to South America where there is support for Buenos Aires’s sovereignty claim.
In a tandem move to kill off Sea Lion, Argentina is expected within 24 hours to escalate further its dispute with the UK by requesting arbitration under annexe VII of the UN convention on the law of the sea (Unclos) over the oil project.
On 28 September, Milei gave the UK a two-week deadline to stop the project or face such a legal action. The deadline passed on Monday and Argentinian newspapers said an application for arbitration would follow.
Under it, Buenos Aires will claim that the UK is in breach of a UN resolution inviting the parties to negotiate over the sovereignty dispute and refrain from “unilateral modifications” to the situation. It will be seeking a binding ruling that the UK must stop the drilling. However, UK government sources are confident that Unclos will not wade into a sovereignty dispute.
At a public meeting on Monday evening, one of the Falkland Islands’ assembly members, Dean Dent, told constituents that the UK government was working hard on a tough response to the Argentinian Unclos threat.
“The UK government has assembled quite an in-depth team of legal advisers, KCs – that is the first step,” he said. “There have been four recent similar cases where a case of sovereignty has been taken to Unclos and all four were disregarded by the tribunal as all four cases were a sovereignty issue, not a maritime issue.”
The UK government is expected to be increasingly muscular in its approach to Argentina in the coming days. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, told parliament on Monday that he had raised the issue and “the clear and declared will of the islanders to remain British” with the US president, Donald Trump.
